At temperature 0 every seed writes the same text; at 0.4, 52% of pairs of seeds are still together after one token and 16 of 20 texts are distinct; at 1.0, 34% and all 20, with 95% of texts containing a token GPT-2 gave under 0.1%. Top-40 at temperature 1 keeps 19.8 distinct texts and cuts that to 2%; top-p 0.9 removes few such tokens here. The same seed and settings reproduce the same text exactly. Unlikeliness under GPT-2 itself stands in for junk; nobody judged the texts.
title: One prompt, many seeds
summary: A language model gives the same chances for the next word every time; the seed supplies the number that picks one, so different seeds write different texts, sooner and more wildly as temperature rises, while cutting off the unlikely tail keeps the variety without the junk.

name: frequentist-and-bayesian
description: A Poisson count of 3. The exact confidence belt, read across at 3, gives 1.37 to 5.92; the posterior from a flat prior gives 2.09 to 5.92. For every count from 0 to 20 the upper ends agree exactly. The confidence interval holds the truth at least 68.3% of the time for every true mean, while the credible interval ranges from 53% to 83%; at a true mean of 3, 20,000 pseudo-experiments give 87.1% and 76.8% (exact 86.6% and 76.5%). With a known background of 3 and no events seen, the confidence interval for the signal is entirely negative, while a posterior whose prior is zero below zero gives 0.17 to 1.84. Central intervals only.
title: Two readings of one count
summary: One small count read twice, as the range of true rates for which that count would be unsurprising and as an updated belief about the rate: where the two answers agree, where they part, and what each one claims.

name: bayes-theorem-areas
description: Exact areas for a disease in 1 in 1,000 people and a test positive for 99% of the ill and 5% of the healthy: of 100,000 people, 99 true positives against 4,995 false ones, so a positive result is right 1.94% of the time; testing again gives 28.2%, then 88.6%. A kaon tag in a sample of 10% kaons, with 90% efficiency and 5% of pions mistaken for kaons, has a purity of 66.7%; 100,000 seeded particles give 66.2%. At 1 kaon in 1,000 the purity is 1.8%, or 31.1% if only 0.2% of pions are mistaken. The rates are round illustrative numbers, and repeated tests are assumed independent.
title: Bayes' theorem as areas
summary: A population drawn as a square, split by how common something is and by how a test comes out, so the chance that a positive result is right is one rectangle compared with two: for a rare disease, and for picking out one kind of particle.

name: prior-washing-out
description: One seeded run of 100,000 flips of a coin with a 0.7 chance of heads updates five priors exactly: flat, optimistic, sceptical, narrow, and dogmatic (zero outside 0.4 to 0.6). The distance from the sceptical posterior to the flat prior's is 0.65 after 10 flips, 0.56 after 100 and 0.18 after 1,000. After 100,000 flips the optimistic and sceptical posteriors are within 0.02 of it, the narrow one is still 0.11 away, and the dogmatic one is as far away as it can be, with its mean stuck at 0.600. The spread over 50 other runs is drawn.
title: A prior washing out
summary: Three people with different starting beliefs about a coin watch the same flips and end up agreeing, while someone who ruled the truth out in advance never can.

name: interval-coverage
description: Of 10,000 seeded Gaussian measurements, 68.0% of the one-sigma intervals contain the true value (70 of the first 100). For a count quoted as n ± root n at a true mean of 2.5, only counts of 2, 3 and 4 give an interval containing 2.5: 60.4% exactly. Over true means from 0.05 to 20 that recipe covers between 5% and 81%, while the exact interval never falls below 68.7%. For an efficiency from 20 trials the usual binomial error bar covers as little as 9% and has zero width at 20 of 20; the Clopper-Pearson interval never covers less than 68.4%. The exact intervals cover more than they promise.
title: What coverage means
summary: Many repeated experiments each draw their error bar around a value we secretly know: a 68% interval is a recipe that works 68% of the time, and the usual quick error bars on small counts do not.

name: binomial-poisson-gaussian
description: Exact distributions, with 20,000 seeded rows of ten trials as a check. The distance between a binomial with mean 3 and a Poisson of mean 3 falls from 0.086 at 10 trials to 0.0008 at 1,000; with the chance held at 0.3 it does not fall at all. A Poisson against a Gaussian of the same mean and width: 0.14 at a mean of 1, where the Gaussian puts 6.7% on negative counts, 0.040 at 10 and 0.004 at 1,000. In the upper tail at a mean of 10, a five-sigma count has an exact probability 37 times the Gaussian's; the factor is 5.1 at a mean of 100 and 1.8 at 1,000.
title: Binomial, Poisson, Gaussian
summary: The count of events in one bin, followed as one histogram that turns from the many-rare-chances shape into the bell curve, with a look at the far tails, where the bell curve stays badly wrong.

name: central-limit-theorem
description: Exact distributions of the mean of 1, 2, 5 and 30 dice, and 20,000 seeded pseudo-experiments for each number averaged from 1 to 100, for dice, exponential decay times and Breit-Wigner draws. The spread of the mean matches sigma over root N within 3%. The exact distance to a Gaussian for decay times falls from 0.159 for one to 0.024 for 30 and 0.013 for 100. For the Breit-Wigner the width of the mean stays at 1.00, 0.99 and 0.99 for 1, 30 and 100 draws, and running means over 10,000 draws are still moving by 2.7 to 21.6 across the last 9,000.
title: The central limit theorem
summary: Averages of dice rolls, then of lopsided decay times, pile up into the same bell shape, narrowing as more are averaged; except for one kind of distribution whose average never settles at all.

name: chi-square-fit
description: Six points with unequal Gaussian errors, drawn from a known line. Chi-square is evaluated exactly over the intercept and slope: a trial line scores 45.8 and the least-squares solution 2.68, for 4 degrees of freedom. The contour one unit above the minimum, found on a grid without the covariance formula, has half-widths 0.297 and 0.0762 against the formula's 0.298 and 0.0766. In 10,000 pseudo-experiments the fitted intercept lies within its error of the truth 68.1% of the time, and the pair lies inside the contour 39.7% of the time (39.3% exact). For a straight line the bowl is an exact paraboloid; for other models it is an approximation.
title: Chi-square as a landscape
summary: A straight line through a few points: each point pulls on the line like a spring, the pulls add up to chi-square, and that sum is a bowl whose bottom is the best fit and whose width gives the errors.

name: chi-square-per-dof
description: Twelve points drawn from a parabola with Gaussian errors. A straight line gives a chi-square of 46.1 for 10 degrees of freedom (probability 1.4 in a million), the parabola 3.5 for 9, and a seventh-degree polynomial 1.3 for 4. Over 20,000 pseudo-experiments the parabola's chi-square follows the exact curve for 9 degrees of freedom. Chi-square per degree of freedom does not flag the fit with too many parameters; what does is that each parameter beyond the needed one lowers chi-square by only 1.00 on average, and the fitted curve ends further from the truth (0.82 against 0.50 errors). With error bars claimed at half, equal to and twice their true size, chi-square per degree of freedom averages 4.01, 1.00 and 0.25.
title: What a good chi-square looks like
summary: The same points fitted with a model that is too simple, the right one and one with too many parameters: what chi-square should be, how the fit probability is read off its distribution, and what wrong error bars do to it.

name: minimisers-on-chi-square
description: A one-peak model fitted for position and width to 24 Poisson counts that also contain a neighbouring peak, so chi-square has two minima: 178 at the right peak and 353 at the neighbour. Gradient descent, Newton's method without safeguards, the simplex and a variable-metric method of the kind MINUIT runs start from 1,035 points. They reach the best fit from 46%, 8%, 60% and 44% of starts and the wrong bottom from 31%, 3%, 25% and 25%, in a median of 75, 35, 59 and 68 evaluations. Where the curvature is negative, Newton's method jumps to a negative width. The model lacks the neighbour by construction, so even its best fit is poor.
title: How a minimiser walks
summary: Three ways of walking downhill on the same chi-square surface, counting every evaluation, on a surface with a second, wrong bottom that traps the starts on its side.

name: binned-vs-unbinned-fits
description: Decay times from an exponential with a lifetime of 2.2 microseconds, fitted by a binned chi-square with errors of root n from the data, a binned Poisson likelihood and an unbinned likelihood; 4,000 pseudo-experiments per setting. In ten bins the chi-square lifetime is biased by +12% at 30 events, -3.7% at 120 (a third of its spread), -1.7% at 1,000 and -0.3% at 4,000, while the likelihoods are within 0.7% from 120 events. The sign changes because empty bins are left out at small samples. The unbinned fit's spread is within 4% of the best possible from 120 events up; with only two bins, both binned fits spread 1.33 times wider. The chi-square with errors from the fitted curve was not run.
title: Binned or unbinned?
summary: One sample of decay times fitted three ways: why a chi-square fit to a histogram with few events per bin gives a biased lifetime while likelihood fits do not, and what binning costs in precision.

name: likelihood-curve
description: Five decay times drawn from an exponential with a lifetime of 2.2 microseconds. The likelihood, evaluated exactly, peaks at 1.675 microseconds, against a sample mean of 1.676. With 20 and 80 events of the same run the curve narrows and its peak sits at 2.08 and 1.87. In 20,000 pseudo-experiments of five decays per seed, three seeds, the best lifetime averages 2.203 and spreads by 0.992, against the exact 0.984, and its histogram follows the exact distribution of a mean of five exponentials.
title: The likelihood curve
summary: Each measured decay time gets a probability from the model; multiply them, slide the lifetime, and the product peaks at the best estimate.

name: likelihood-intervals
description: Decay times from an exponential with a lifetime of 2.2 microseconds. With 50 decays the curvature of the log-likelihood gives an error of 0.367 and the half-unit drop gives -0.33 +0.40; with 5 decays, -1.14 +2.08 against a symmetric 1.50. Coverage comes from 20,000 pseudo-experiments per seed and from the exact distribution, which agree within 0.6 points. Against the textbook expectation, the symmetric interval does not cover worse in total at 5 decays (67.8% against 67.4%); what differs is the side it misses on: it lies wholly below the truth 27% of the time and above it 5%, where the half-unit interval gives 20% and 13%.
title: Errors from the likelihood
summary: The error on a fitted value is read off where the log-likelihood has dropped by one half, and with few events that interval is lopsided.

name: error-propagation
description: Two Gaussian measurements, 10.0 ± 0.5 and 5.00 ± 0.25, and their ratio; 100,000 pairs per seed, five seeds. The formula gives 0.141 and the cloud 0.142. With a correlation of 0.6 the formula with its correlation term gives 0.089 and the cloud 0.090; without the term it is 57% too large. With the denominator known only to 30% the formula says 2.00 ± 0.61, while the cloud's central 68% is -0.47 +0.86: 83% wider upwards than downwards. In that case the cloud's standard deviation never settles between seeds, because a ratio with a Gaussian denominator has no finite variance, so half-widths are reported instead.
title: Error propagation by cloud
summary: A cloud of possible measurements is pushed through a formula; the usual error formula matches the cloud only while the function is nearly straight over the errors.

name: error-on-the-mean
description: Gaussian measurements with a spread of 2; 10,000 experiments at each size from 1 to 1,024 measurements, three seeds. The spread of the mean is 1.997, 1.000, 0.499 and 0.251 for 1, 4, 16 and 64 measurements, a slope of -0.500 on log axes, within 3% of sigma over root N everywhere; a lopsided distribution of the same spread follows the same line. Dividing the summed squared deviations by N gives 75.0% of the true variance at four measurements, by N - 1 gives 100.0%, and the standard deviation itself still averages 92.1% of the truth.
title: The error on the mean
summary: Repeat an experiment many times and its average scatters far less than single measurements do, shrinking as one over the square root of how many you take.

name: bootstrap-errors
description: One dataset of 20 events, resampled 2,000 times with replacement, for a mean, a median, a ratio of means, a correlation and a maximum; the true spread of each comes from 20,000 fresh datasets per seed. Over 400 datasets the bootstrap error is typically 0.91, 1.02, 0.96 and 0.87 of the true spread for the first four, with a wide band from one dataset to another (about 0.6 to 1.4). It fails for the maximum: 63% of resamples return the sample's own largest value, and the error is typically 41% of the truth. The dataset drawn has one unusually large event, so its own numbers for the mean are about 45% high; the animation shows the 400-dataset result beside them.
title: The bootstrap
summary: With one dataset and no formula, draw from the data itself over and over; how much the recomputed answer varies is the error.

name: error-ellipse
description: A straight line is fitted to five points with Gaussian noise of 0.5, 20,000 times per seed over three seeds. The covariance of the fitted intercept and slope matches the exact matrix to the third decimal place, with a correlation of -0.905. The chi-square + 1 contour of a single fit matches the cloud's ellipse to within 0.8% and holds the true pair in 39.8% of fits (39.3% exact), while the intercept's own error bar holds the true intercept in 68.5%. With the slope refitted the intercept is known to 0.524; with the slope held, to 0.224. Counting x from the middle of the data removes the tilt: correlation -0.01.
section: U. Correlated errors and systematic uncertainties (4)
title: The error ellipse
summary: Fitting a line gives two numbers whose errors are tied together, and the tilt of their cloud says how.

name: statistical-vs-systematic
description: Each event is 100 plus a shift shared by the whole run plus Gaussian noise of 10; the shift is known only as 0 ± 0.5. Over 4,000 runs per seed and three seeds, the distance of the mean from the truth follows the two errors added in quadrature to within 4%: 0.71 at 400 events, where the two are equal, and 0.509 at 10,000. An interval built from the statistical error alone holds the truth 52% of the time at 400 events and 16% at 10,000; with the total error, 68 to 69%. Measuring the shift on a control sample a quarter the size gives an error that keeps falling, and beats the uncorrected one from 1,600 events; below that it is worse. The run drawn ends 0.61 above the truth, a two-sigma fluctuation on top of its shift of 0.4.
section: U. Correlated errors and systematic uncertainties (4)
title: Statistical against systematic error
summary: More data shrinks the scatter of an average but not a miscalibration shared by every event, unless the miscalibration is itself measured.

name: nuisance-parameters-profiling
description: A count with 20 signal events expected at a signal strength of 1, on a background known as 50 ± 10. For the first pseudo-experiment, which counts 80, the signal strength is 1.07 to 1.96 with the background fixed at 50, missing the true value, 0.84 to 2.18 profiled and 0.86 to 2.21 marginalised. Over 20,000 pseudo-experiments per seed in which the true background varies within its uncertainty, the interval holds the true signal strength in 48.9% of cases with the background fixed, 68.1% profiled and 68.3% marginalised; exact sums give 48.5%, 68.0% and 68.2%.
section: U. Correlated errors and systematic uncertainties (4)
title: Profiling a nuisance parameter
summary: When a background is only roughly known, pretending it is exact gives an error bar that is too small; profiling it gives an honest one.

name: combining-measurements
description: Two measurements of a true value of 10, with errors 1.0 and 2.6 and a shared shift that correlates them by 0.74; 20,000 pairs per seed, three seeds. Weighting by one over the error squared, as if independent, quotes ± 0.93 but scatters by 1.14, worse than the better measurement alone (1.00), and holds the truth 59.1% of the time. The best linear combination has weights 1.235 and -0.235, scatters by 0.88, holds the truth 68.4% of the time, and always lies outside both inputs. Exactly, the second weight is zero at a correlation of 0.385, the ratio of the two errors, and negative beyond.
section: U. Correlated errors and systematic uncertainties (4)
title: Combining measurements
summary: Two results that share a source of error must not be averaged as if independent; the best combination can even lie outside both.

name: moving-a-cut
description: Pseudo-data: 50 signal events on 1,000 background events, both Gaussian, one unit apart in a single variable. Keeping events above 1 leaves 43 signal and 164 background. From the model exactly, s over root (s + b) is best at a cut of 1.96, the likelihood-ratio formula at 2.47 and s over root b at 3.33, where it claims 7.0 sigma on 0.43 background events against 3.7 from the exact Poisson probability; purity only rises, so its best cut keeps nothing. Over 5,000 pseudo-experiments the estimated signal averages 50.1 with a cut fixed beforehand and 67.1 with the cut that looks best on the same events; with no signal, an excess past 2 sigma appears in 2.6% and 15.3% of them.
title: Moving a cut
summary: A cut slides across a signal and a background histogram, and the counts, purity and significance follow it, with each measure of best picking a different cut.

name: cuts-vs-multivariate
description: Pseudo-data: two Gaussian clouds correlated by 0.8, the signal shifted in the first variable only. Selections are chosen on 5,000 events of each kind and measured on 20,000 others, over five seeds. At 80% signal efficiency the best pair of thresholds keeps 43.8% of the background, no better than the first variable alone (43.3%); Fisher's line, computed from the means and the pooled covariance, keeps 20.5%, and is below the cuts at every efficiency from 5% to 95%. In a second model with a crescent of signal round a blob, the best line keeps 27.3% and a contour of the model's own likelihood ratio 2.1%; that contour is taken from the model, not learned.
title: Cuts against a combined variable
summary: Two thresholds, one on each of two correlated variables, compared with a single diagonal line through both, and then with a curved boundary where no line will do.

name: sideband-background
description: Pseudo-data: 6,000 background events on a falling exponential with a Gaussian peak of 300 at 125 GeV. The background is fitted in the sidebands only and carried under the peak: in the spectrum drawn, 1,324 events in the window less a background of 1,011 ± 19 gives 313 ± 41, where the truth in the window is 296. Over 5,000 spectra per case the estimate is off by -1.5 events with the right shape, and the quoted error is right 68.4% of the time; by -96 events (2.3 sigma) when a straight line is fitted to the curved background; and by -34 events when the peak is wide enough for 32% of it to fall outside the window.
title: Background from the sidebands
summary: The background under a peak is estimated by fitting the spectrum on either side of it, and the estimate goes wrong when the assumed shape is wrong or the sides contain signal.

name: selection-sculpting
description: Pseudo-data: 200,000 events on a falling exponential, a trigger that turns on around 30 GeV, and a detector that sees part of the solid angle. The recorded spectrum peaks at 36 to 40 GeV; the truth has no peak. Dividing by an efficiency measured on a calibration sample recovers the truth above 38 GeV to within 0.1% on average over 4,000 pseudo-experiments, with errors of 2 to 5%; where the efficiency is 0.1% the error is 59% and the estimate is biased high by 28%. In a second model of pairs with no resonance, requiring both momenta above a threshold puts a peak in the mass spectrum that moves up by about 2 GeV per GeV of threshold. The acceptance here is flat in energy, so the trigger does all the sculpting of the first spectrum.
title: How a selection sculpts a spectrum
summary: A trigger threshold and a detector's acceptance turn a smoothly falling spectrum into one with a peak, and a cut on momentum does the same to a mass spectrum.

name: type-i-and-type-ii-errors
description: A counting experiment with 10 background events expected if there is no signal and 18 if there is. Rejecting the no-signal hypothesis at 16 or more events, the smallest threshold with a false-alarm rate of at most 5%, gives by exact Poisson sums a false-alarm rate of 4.87%, a miss rate of 28.7% and a power of 71.3%; 5,000 pseudo-experiments under each hypothesis gave 4.8% and 27.3%. With the threshold chosen again for each amount of data, power is 71.3% at one run, 89.8% at two and 99.4% at four. Counts are whole numbers, so the false-alarm rate sits between 3.1% and 5.0% and the power curve has steps.
title: Two ways for a test to be wrong
summary: A counting experiment under two hypotheses and a threshold on the count: the two kinds of error as the parts of each distribution on the wrong side, traded against each other as the threshold slides.

name: p-values
description: Ten measurements with errors of 2.0 against a prediction of 20 give a chi-square of 24.92. Of 20,000 pseudo-experiments with nothing to find, 104 reach that value (p = 0.0052); the exact tail for 10 degrees of freedom is 0.0055, or 2.54 sigma one-sided. The p-values of those pseudo-experiments are flat: 4.98% fall below 0.05. In a population where 10% of experiments have a real effect of that size, a stated assumption, 41% of the results with p below 0.05 are false alarms.
title: What a p-value is, and is not
summary: One measured result set against the distribution it would have if there were nothing to find, then why a small p-value is not the chance that there is nothing to find.

name: neyman-pearson
description: Two hypotheses about a pair of independent Gaussian measurements. At a false-alarm rate of 5% the exact power is 44.2% cutting on the first value alone, 54.0% on their sum and 60.9% on the likelihood ratio; 20,000 pseudo-events of each hypothesis give 44.2%, 53.6% and 60.7%. Over every direction of straight cut the power peaks at the likelihood ratio's own direction, and a different function that rises with the ratio passes exactly the same events. With equal spreads under both hypotheses the best boundary is a straight line, so curved regions are not shown.
title: The likelihood ratio is the best test
summary: Three ways to turn two measured values into one test, cut to the same false-alarm rate: the likelihood ratio catches the most signal, and no other direction of cut does better.

name: look-elsewhere-effect
description: A falling background of 60 bins with no signal, scanned with a four-bin window at 57 positions, in 100,000 pseudo-experiments. The largest local excess passes 3 sigma in 5.2% of spectra against 0.135% for one fixed window, a trials factor of 38, which corresponds to about 43 independent places; treating all 57 overlapping windows as independent would give 6.8%. A local 3 sigma is a global 1.63 sigma and a local 4 sigma a global 3.03. The spectrum drawn is the first of the 100,000 with a window past 3 sigma, and says so. No spectrum reached a local 5 sigma, so that row is an extrapolation and is labelled as one.
title: The look-elsewhere effect
summary: A spectrum with nothing in it still shows a striking excess somewhere when enough places are searched; many such spectra show how often, and what a local significance is worth after the search.

name: bump-hunt
description: One pseudo-data spectrum: about 3,000 background events on a falling exponential with 70 signal events injected at 125. Fits without and with a signal give 86 ± 22 signal events and a likelihood-ratio statistic of 16.76, a local significance of 4.09 sigma. Over 100,000 background-only spectra that statistic is zero in 50.2% and passes 1, 2 and 3 sigma in 15.9%, 2.23% and 0.107% (exact 15.9%, 2.28%, 0.135%). Scanning 49 masses, 15 of 20,000 background-only scans reach 4.09 sigma somewhere: a global significance of 3.17 sigma, a trials factor of about 35. The spectrum drawn fluctuated upwards: the typical significance for this signal is 3.30 sigma. The global figure rests on 15 pseudo-experiments.
section: X. Discoveries, exclusion and upper limits (5)
title: A bump hunt, from fit to global significance
summary: One mass spectrum followed from the background fit to a bump's local significance, and then to what that significance is worth once every mass has been searched.

name: poisson-upper-limits
description: Exact Poisson arithmetic: the 90% upper limits on a signal mean are 2.30, 3.89, 5.32 and 6.68 for 0, 1, 2 and 3 events seen. With a known background of 3 the limit is that less 3, which is negative when no events are seen. Coverage is checked with 20,000 counts at each of 40 true signals: never below 89.7% (exactly, never below 90.0%) and 95.0% on average, because counts are whole numbers. One worked line turns the limit into a cross-section: with 20 inverse femtobarns and an efficiency of 0.25, no events seen means less than 0.46 femtobarns.
section: X. Discoveries, exclusion and upper limits (5)
title: An upper limit from counting
summary: Seeing few or no events still rules out large signals: where the famous 2.3 comes from, and what the 90% promises.

name: cls-method
description: A counting experiment with a known background of 10 at 95% confidence. Seeing 4 events, a chosen example, the plain limit on the signal is -0.85 and the CLs limit 4.28. Over 100,000 background-only counts the plain method excludes signals of 0, 1 and 2 events in 2.9%, 6.7% and 12.9% of experiments; CLs never does, since its limit never falls below 3.0. The price is coverage above what is promised: never under 95.2%, and 100% for a signal of 0.5, with a typical limit of 8.08 against 6.96.
section: X. Discoveries, exclusion and upper limits (5)
title: The CLs method
summary: When fewer events turn up than the background alone predicts, the plain limit rules out signals the experiment could never see; dividing by a second tail area repairs that, at a price.

name: brazil-band
description: Twelve counting windows across a mass range, each with a known falling background and a model signal; limits are 95% CLs limits divided by the model's prediction. From 5,000 background-only counts per mass, the point at 120 has a median of 0.87, a 68% band of 0.60 to 1.17 and a 95% band of 0.46 to 1.66. An observed limit from one pseudo-dataset with the model injected at 140 is 2.47 there against 0.91 expected, the only point outside the yellow band. Over 20,000 background-only plots a given point is outside the yellow band 3.9% of the time, not 5%, because counts are whole numbers, and at least one of the twelve is outside in 38% of plots.
section: X. Discoveries, exclusion and upper limits (5)
title: The bands of a limit plot
summary: The green and yellow bands show the range of limits an experiment would set if there were nothing to find, built here one pseudo-experiment at a time and then compared with an observed limit.

name: why-five-sigma
description: A search of 20 independent bins with a known flat background, looked at 30 times as data accumulate. A signal of 5 events per unit of data reaches 5.6 sigma by the end; the largest background-only bin peaks at 2.3 sigma and fades to 1.1. Over 100,000 background-only searches, one bin at the last look reaches 3 sigma in 0.12%, any of the 20 bins at any look in 19.9%, and at least one of ten such searches in 89%; five sigma is reached somewhere in 4 of 100,000. The exact one-sided tails are 1 in 741 and 1 in 3.5 million. The data needed for a typical five-sigma result is 103, 27 and 8 units for signals of 2.5, 5 and 10 events per unit.
section: X. Discoveries, exclusion and upper limits (5)
title: Why five sigma
summary: As data accumulate a real signal keeps growing while chance bumps rise and fade, and with many places and moments to look, three sigma turns up routinely and five almost never.

name: network-regression
description: Real MNIST digits stand in for events: each is turned by a known angle within 45 degrees either way and read as 7 by 7 cells, as an analysis would regress a particle's energy from detector readings. A network with one linear output, trained with squared error on 10,000 digits over five seeds, has a held-out resolution of 11.2 degrees (10.9 to 11.3), against 26.0 for always answering zero. The resolution is flat across the range, but the bias is +10.3 degrees at the lowest angles and -7.6 at the highest: answers are pulled towards the middle of the range.
section: Y. Machine learning in a physics analysis (4)
title: Regression with a network
summary: A network with one unsquashed output learns to give back the angle a digit was turned by, and its errors show its resolution and bias.

name: classifier-score-as-variable
description: MNIST 4s stand for signal and 9s for background, read coarsely so the classes overlap. On held-out digits the network's ROC area is 0.953 over five seeds. A cut at 0.5 keeps 81% of signal and rejects 94% of background: 93% pure with equal numbers, 22% pure at one signal event per fifty background. There the cut that maximises significance moves from about 0.4 to about 0.95. Fitting the score's shape recovers signal fractions of 0.05 to 0.5 to within 0.006 over 2,000 pseudo-experiments each, with a smaller spread than counting above a cut. The one-in-fifty numbers are scaled shares, so the background above a cut of 0.95 rests on about ten held-out digits.
section: Y. Machine learning in a physics analysis (4)
title: A classifier's score as a variable
summary: A network's score separates signal from background; a cut on it trades efficiency for purity, and its shape can be fitted for how much signal a sample holds.

name: boosted-regression-trees
description: On the same turned digits as the regression network. With one real feature, the tilt of the ink, and 300 training digits, the training error falls from 25.5 degrees to 22.9, 21.0 and 18.5 after 1, 2 and 50 small trees, while the held-out error is lowest after 10 trees. On all 49 cells with 10,000 digits, 300 trees and three seeds, the held-out error runs from 18.4 degrees to 12.1 over twelve settings of learning rate and depth. More trees do not overfit at small learning rates within 300 trees; at a rate of 1 they do, from 10 trees on at depth 5. The network on the same events gets 11.2 degrees, ahead of the best trees in every seed.
section: Y. Machine learning in a physics analysis (4)
title: Boosted trees for regression
summary: Small trees are added one at a time, each fitted to what the sum so far still gets wrong, first on one measured number and then on a whole detector read-out.

name: overtraining-check
description: A large network trained on 25 to 2,000 MNIST 4s and 9s per class, five seeds, compared on its training events and on about 5,800 held-out ones. With 100 per class every training score ends in the outermost bins while 10% of held-out 4s sit at the wrong end. The Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance between the two score distributions falls from 0.36 at 25 per class to 0.04 at 2,000, and the gap in ROC area from 0.128 to 0.013. Stopping early or weight decay roughly halves the distance at 100 per class. Against the usual telling, overtraining barely lowers the held-out ROC area here (0.927 to 0.921) while the validation loss triples: it spoils what the score means, not the ranking.
section: Y. Machine learning in a physics analysis (4)
title: The overtraining check
summary: The scores of the events a classifier was trained on are laid over those of events it never saw; where they part, it has learnt its sample rather than the rule.

name: autoencoder-anomaly-detection
description: An autoencoder is trained on 20,000 MNIST digits with one class removed entirely, for each of the ten classes, seven code sizes and three seeds; the removed class stands for new physics in a model-independent search trained on known processes. Each of 5,000 held-out digits is scored by its reconstruction error. With the 0s removed and a code of 8 numbers, 74% of the unseen 0s are flagged where 95% of seen digits pass; area under the ROC curve 0.95. By removed class the area runs from 0.95 for 0 and 2, through 0.76 for 7 and 0.63 for 9, down to 0.32 for 1, worse than a coin toss on every seed: an unseen 1 is rebuilt better than a typical seen digit. The mean area peaks at a code of 8 (0.81) and falls to 0.62 at 128: a roomy code rebuilds unseen digits too. The code size drawn is the best one, chosen on the held-out digits, which a real search could not do.
section: Z. Anomalies, collapse and smooth backgrounds (5)
title: Anomaly detection with an autoencoder
summary: An autoencoder trained without one kind of digit rebuilds that kind badly, and the size of the error flags what it never saw.

name: gan-mode-collapse
description: A small GAN is trained on 20,000 MNIST digits in four settings, five seeds each, and a separately trained classifier reads 1,000 of its samples every 100 updates. With one generator update per discriminator update it ends covering 8.7 of the ten digits; with three, the only change, it covers 1.9 and all five seeds collapse, each onto a digit of its own, hopping between digits on the way. Given the label as an extra input to both networks, the generator-heavy runs cover 7.8 digits and none collapses, and 73 to 77% of samples are read as the digit asked for, against 10% by chance. That is not every class on demand: a longer one-seed run reached 92%. Samples at this size are rough.
section: Z. Anomalies, collapse and smooth backgrounds (5)
title: Mode collapse in a GAN
summary: A generator that settles on a few digits instead of all ten, counted by a separate classifier, and how telling both networks the label brings the digits back.

name: gp-background-fit
description: Pseudo-data: a falling spectrum of about 98,000 events in 80 bins whose true shape is a sum of two exponentials, fitted with a single exponential and with a Gaussian process on top of that fit; 4,000 pseudo-experiments with and without an injected resonance of 160 events, at 13 length scales, each beside the exact calculation. With no signal the single exponential leaves -21.8 events at 300 GeV, and up to almost 7 errors of spurious signal elsewhere; the process at a length scale of 60 GeV leaves +1.7 and stays within one error everywhere. Of the injected signal the exponential keeps 92%, the process 65% at 60 GeV and 3% at 10 GeV. The background is fitted to the whole spectrum, signal region included.
section: Z. Anomalies, collapse and smooth backgrounds (5)
title: A Gaussian-process background
summary: A fixed function leaves a wave that looks like signal; a Gaussian process follows the background instead, but a short length scale swallows a real bump.

name: anomaly-loss-and-latent
description: The autoencoders of autoencoder-anomaly-detection, trained on MNIST with one class removed, for each of the ten classes and three seeds; the removed class stands for new physics in a model-independent search. Each of 5,000 held-out digits gets a reconstruction error and the distance from its code to the 5th nearest training code. With a code of 8 numbers the areas under the ROC curve are 0.81 for the loss and 0.69 for the distance. For the unseen 1s the loss gives 0.32 and the distance 0.78: their codes do sit apart, but with each threshold passing 95% of normal digits only 19% are caught, by the code alone, and 80% by neither. Over all removed classes 36% are caught by the loss only, 11% by the code only, 4% by both and 50% by neither. Of eight ways of spoiling a digit, inverted ones are caught by both, noisy, shifted and turned ones by the loss alone, and dimmed or averaged ones by neither. A Mahalanobis distance scores 0.29, worse than a coin toss; the neighbour distance was chosen over it after seeing these areas. Thresholds use normal digits only.
section: Z. Anomalies, collapse and smooth backgrounds (5)
title: Two places an anomaly can show
summary: One picture through an autoencoder gets two scores, how badly it is rebuilt and how far its code lies from the training codes, and an unusual input can show in both, in one or in neither.

name: anomaly-two-score-flow
description: The same autoencoders at code sizes 2, 8, 32 and 128, ten removed classes and three seeds. A Gaussian, a mixture of ten and a small normalizing flow are fitted to the training codes; the mixture fits held-out normal codes best and is used, a choice made without anomalies. As anomaly scores their areas are 0.29, 0.63 and 0.56, and a plain neighbour distance beats all three (0.69). At 5% false alarms the loss alone catches 40% of anomalies, the code alone 12%, either cut 32%, a sum of the two 22% and an ellipse round the normal cloud 4%. On average the second score buys nothing at 8 numbers; its gain is the class the loss cannot see, the unseen 1s, from 0.4% caught to 7%. Two cuts at 5% each flag 10.2% of normal digits, so each is set at 2.6%. As the code grows the loss's area falls from 0.81 to 0.62 while the code density's rises from 0.63 to 0.86 at 32 numbers: the anomaly moves from the loss into the code, though not for the 1s. The flow is small and not a strong representative of flows.
section: Z. Anomalies, collapse and smooth backgrounds (5)
title: An anomaly search with two scores
summary: The whole procedure from training on normal data to a decision: a density fitted to the codes, two thresholds set on normal data, three ways of combining the two scores, and what a second cut costs in false alarms.

name: cpu-and-gpu-training
description: A classifier of about 100,000 weights and an autoencoder of 5.4 million, 71 times the arithmetic per step, trained on MNIST. The speeds shown are representative round figures for an ordinary desktop CPU and a separate mid-range graphics card, not measurements, and every phase that shows one says so: per training step on 128 digits, 1 ms on the CPU and 0.5 ms on the GPU for the classifier, 40 ms and 2 ms for the autoencoder. So the autoencoder is 40 times slower than the classifier on the CPU and 4 times slower on the GPU, yet on the GPU it is still 20 times faster than on the CPU, while the small classifier gains only 2 times because fixed costs are most of its GPU step. Time against batch size follows a simple stated cost model. By arithmetic from those figures, twenty passes over the data take the autoencoder 6.2 minutes on the CPU and 19 seconds on the GPU, and a model 100 times larger on 1,000 times the data 433 days and 22 days. A phase on precision shows how many bits a number gets, from 64 down to 4, exactly, and representative speeds at each width: a CPU is built for 64-bit and does 64-bit sums at full speed, while a graphics card is built for 32-bit, does 16-, 8- and 4-bit sums 4 to 16 times faster and 64-bit at 1/64 of its 32-bit rate, below the CPU's. Stored in 16 or 8 bits, the trained classifier keeps its 97.3% held-out accuracy; in plain 4-bit 99% of its weights round to zero and it falls to 23.2%, and with one shared scale per 32 weights it is back at 97.2%. Only the learning curves and those accuracies are measured, on held-out MNIST digits.
title: Training on a CPU and on a GPU
summary: Where a model's weights and a batch of digits sit in a computer, where the arithmetic happens with and without a GPU, and how long a small and a larger model typically take to train on each.

name: tree-splits-and-impurity
description: MNIST 4s stand for signal and 9s for background, with two measured features so the split can be drawn. On twelve real events every threshold of both features is scored by Gini, entropy and misclassification error: the best takes Gini from 0.500 to 0.143. With 2,000 training events the best threshold on the ink's vertical spread gains 0.265 against 0.206 for the best on the other feature, and all three criteria choose the same root in each of five seeds. Further down they differ: at one real node no threshold lowers the error while Gini still gains 0.032, and that happens at 20% of Gini's nodes. Whole trees on 49 features have a held-out error of 9.1% grown with Gini, 9.0% with entropy and 11.8% with misclassification error, which stops early.
section: a. Decision trees, forests and boosting (10)
title: Choosing a split
summary: How a tree node picks its question: every threshold on every feature is scored by how much purer it leaves the two sides, and the best one wins.

name: tree-pruning-and-depth
description: On two features of 500 training digits, a tree grown until nothing can be split has 58 leaves, no training error and a held-out error of 14.6%. Cut at depth 3 it has 8 leaves and 11.3%; with at least 20 events per leaf, 11.3%; with a minimum gain, 7 leaves and 10.9%. Cost-complexity pruning gives nine nested trees from 58 leaves to 1, and five-fold cross-validation picks the one with 7 leaves. Over five seeds the fully grown tree is worse than the best depth in every seed (15.1% against 11.1%). On 49 features with 2,000 events the held-out error does not turn up with depth; it flattens, and pruning gains about 0.7 points.
section: a. Decision trees, forests and boosting (10)
title: Holding a tree back
summary: A tree grown until every leaf is pure has learnt its sample; depth limits, leaf sizes, a minimum gain and pruning cut it back to what holds up on new events.

name: tree-instability
description: Four trees grown on resamples of the same 500 digits do not all agree on 17% of held-out events, though each alone is 13 to 14% wrong. Over five seeds two fully grown trees disagree on 12 to 13% of held-out events, against 4 to 7% for one-question trees. Replacing 1% of the training events changes 5% of answers. Over 40 separate training samples the squared bias falls from 0.172 for one question to 0.036 for a full tree while the variance rises from 0.005 to 0.060, and the majority of the 40 trees is 4.3% wrong against 9.6% for one. The first question itself rarely changes (the same feature in 91 to 100% of resamples); the trees part ways from the second question down.
section: a. Decision trees, forests and boosting (10)
title: One tree is unstable
summary: Resample the same training events and a single tree changes its questions and its answers; deep trees are right on average but scatter, which is why many are used.

name: bagging
description: A bootstrap of 16 real events is drawn pick by pick: 12 come up and 4 are left out, and on resamples of 2,000 events 63.2% come up. On 49 features, over 20 separate training samples, the held-out error is 10.8% for one tree, 6.1% for ten and 4.9% for a hundred, falling in every sample. The variance of the vote follows the formula for correlated trees, with a measured correlation of 0.060, to within 3%, and stops at a floor set by that correlation. The out-of-bag error at 100 trees is 5.3% against 4.9% held-out: a little pessimistic, and far too high for small bags (8.2% against 6.1% at ten trees).
section: a. Decision trees, forests and boosting (10)
title: Bagging
summary: Many trees, each grown on a resample of the data, vote: the wobble of single trees averages away, down to the part they all share.

name: random-forest
description: With all 49 features tried at each split, all 100 trees ask about the same cell first; with 7 tried they start from 21 different cells. Over five seeds, as the features tried go from 49 to 1 the correlation between trees falls from 0.30 to 0.11 while single trees get worse (10.7% to 23.0% held-out). The forest's held-out error is 5.6% at 1 feature, 4.4% at 7, 4.1% at 14 and 4.8% at 49, which is bagging: 14 is best in every seed, not the usual square root of 49. One cell holds 18% of the total gain, and shuffling it raises the error from 4.4% to 14.4%; below it the two measures of importance part, with ten cells that each hold over 1% of the gain yet cost under 0.1 points when shuffled.
section: a. Decision trees, forests and boosting (10)
title: A random forest
summary: Bagging with one more trick: each split may only look at a random handful of features, so the trees differ usefully; then which features the forest relies on.

name: adaboost
description: MNIST 4s stand for signal and 9s for background, read as 16 cells. On two cells with 200 events the first one-question tree gets 61 wrong, which gives it a say of 0.41; the events it got wrong then weigh 1.64 times the average, and the next tree is fitted to those weights. The weighted vote of 1, 2, 3, 10 and 100 such trees has a held-out error of 35.6%, 30.9%, 29.5%, 23.1% and 23.3%. On all 16 cells with 2,000 events and five seeds, 400 trees reach 15.6% held-out error and a ROC area of 0.923. The heaviest 1% of events end with 9% of the weight; the eight heaviest are shown as digits. Against the usual telling the margin does not grow here, and with one-question trees the training error never reaches zero.
section: a. Decision trees, forests and boosting (10)
title: AdaBoost: weights on the mistakes
summary: Stumps are fitted one after another, each to events re-weighted so that the last one's mistakes count for more, and their weighted vote carves up the plane.

name: boosting-shrinkage-and-early-stopping
description: Gradient boosting for classification, in numpy, 2,000 rounds over five seeds on MNIST 4s against 9s. The lowest held-out loss is 0.336 at a learning rate of 1 (after about 19 trees), 0.270 at 0.3, 0.266 at 0.1 and 0.265 at 0.03 (after about 1,077): smaller steps need more trees and end lower, though below 0.1 the gain is inside the spread between seeds. Half the rows per tree gives 0.261 against 0.266 for all of them; a tenth, 0.315. Trees three questions deep are best (0.266; one question 0.343, six 0.283). Stopping when the validation loss has not improved for 50 rounds keeps 375 trees and a held-out loss of 0.274, where running all 2,000 gives 0.445.
section: a. Decision trees, forests and boosting (10)
title: Gradient boosting: the settings
summary: Each new tree is fitted to how strongly the loss pulls every event towards its label; small steps, a share of the rows, the right depth and stopping when validation loss turns make it work.

name: xgboost-split-gain
description: The algorithm XGBoost uses, written out in numpy and tested against brute force; no number comes from the library. One event's loss is drawn with its slope and curvature; eight real events as one leaf give a best value of 0.19; a cut slides through them with the sums on each side and the gain, which peaks at 0.21. On a real node, the penalty lambda at 0, 1 and 10 shrinks a leaf value from -1.22 to -0.16 to -0.02, a split fee gamma of 1 refuses the split, and a minimum child weight of 1 forbids 11 of 28 thresholds. Over five seeds, lambda at 10 gives the lowest held-out loss (0.257 against 0.271 with none), while gamma only makes trees smaller. Using the curvature changes which split is chosen at 57% of nodes in later rounds, but makes no measurable difference to the held-out loss here.
section: a. Decision trees, forests and boosting (10)
title: How XGBoost scores a split
summary: Every event carries a slope and a curvature of its loss; a leaf's best value and a split's worth are simple sums of them, read off the bottoms of parabolas.

name: xgboost-histograms-and-missing-values
description: The algorithm XGBoost uses, written out in numpy. For one tree three questions deep on 2,000 events, exact split finding sorts 96,000 readings and scores 45,748 gaps; with 32 bins it scores 1,765 cuts, and the subtraction trick halves the readings added into bins. Held-out loss by number of bins: 0.455 with 2, 0.296 with 8, 0.263 with 32 and with 64, and 0.266 exact. With 30% of readings removed at random, the learnt side for missing values gives 0.404 against 0.425 to 0.429 for a fixed side; when low readings are the ones missing, a fixed side does as well. Growing leaf by leaf shows no advantage over level by level here. On the machine that built it the binned search took about a seventh of the time; that timing varies by machine, the counts do not.
section: a. Decision trees, forests and boosting (10)
title: XGBoost's histograms
summary: Why it is fast: each feature is cut into a few bins once, splits come from bin totals, a child's totals come by subtraction, and missing values go to whichever side gains more.

name: xgboost-one-round
description: The algorithm XGBoost uses, written out in numpy. Round one: eight events with their scores, slopes and curvatures, the root's histograms, the best of 265 cuts, one weak split pruned, leaf values, the step, and the training loss from 0.693 to 0.592. Over 600 rounds the lowest held-out loss is 0.261. Each restraint is then turned on alone from a loose setting that ends at 0.669: a small learning rate gives 0.304, shallow trees 0.277, lambda 0.284, a minimum child weight 0.281, while sampling half the rows does not help (0.691). On the same events over five seeds, held-out error is 19.7% for one tuned tree, 15.6% for AdaBoost, 13.3% for forest-style averaging, 11.4% for gradient boosting and 10.9% for the XGBoost-style method, ahead of gradient boosting in every seed but by under a point.
section: a. Decision trees, forests and boosting (10)
title: One round of XGBoost
summary: One boosting round followed for real events from the current predictions to a new tree and back, then many rounds, the knobs that restrain it, and four other ways to use trees.

name: vae-kl-term
description: A VAE with a code of two numbers is trained on 20,000 MNIST digits and its 2,000 held-out codes are recorded at 14 points in training, coloured by digit, with three seeds. At the start the encoder says nothing, so every code already sits on the prior; reconstruction bursts the cloud apart over the first 40 updates, and the KL term then settles it into the rings: its distance from the bell peaks at 4.4 and falls to 0.10. The cloud becomes more Gaussian-like without becoming a bell: 76% of codes lie inside the second ring against 86% for a Gaussian, and the digits' clusters remain. The same network with no KL term ends 9.3 from the bell with 41% inside the second ring, and rebuilds no better at this size. With the KL term weighted by 0.1 the cloud stays ragged (1.93); weighted by 10 it fits the rings (0.02) but each digit's blob widens five times and reconstruction costs 19 nats more.
title: The KL term of a VAE
summary: One digit followed through a VAE, what the KL half of its loss measures, and the cloud of codes settling into the bell's rings as training goes on.

name: dec-centroids-training
description: K-means on the two-number codes of a trained autoencoder is drawn round by round, then DEC is followed through 1,500 updates at 11 checkpoints, with the held-out codes coloured by digit and the ten centres leaving trails; three seeds. The clusters tighten and separate: the silhouette rises from 0.36 to 0.73 and the assignments sharpen from 0.49 to 0.74. The labels barely follow: cluster accuracy goes from 0.46 to 0.51, because DEC sharpens whatever k-means began with, mistakes included; in the run drawn 4s and 9s, 5s and 8s, and 2s and 3s still share clusters. Keeping the decoder (IDEC) gives the same accuracy and half the reconstruction error (0.042 against 0.081). A ten-number code is no better (0.51), and the outcome depends more on the autoencoder's seed than on where k-means starts. The run drawn, fixed in advance, is the least accurate of the three.
title: DEC: the centroids move
summary: K-means places ten centres in an autoencoder's code space, then DEC pulls the codes and the centres into tight, separate clusters, which are not the same thing as the right ones.

name: entropy-and-gini-by-hand
description: A tree's nodes on all ten MNIST digits, from 10,000 training digits. At the root the ten shares give an entropy of 3.320 bits, all but the 3.322 of an even mix, and a Gini index of 0.900, its 0.9 maximum; each is worked out term by term, -p log2 p and p(1 - p). Gini is the chance that two digits drawn from the node differ: of 200,000 drawn pairs, 0.8998 ± 0.0007 differ. Entropy is the fewest yes/no questions needed on average to name the digit: a Huffman code for the root's counts asks 3.380, within one bit of it, and for a node of 574 digits, 539 of them 7s, it asks 1.125 against an entropy of 0.455, since no code asks less than one question. The first question leaves 2.760 bits on one side and 3.091 on the other, 2.963 weighted, a gain of 0.356; following the yes side five questions down, both measures fall, to 0.455 bits and a Gini of 0.117. For two kinds the measures have one shape; in nats entropy is never below Gini.
title: Entropy and Gini by hand
summary: How impure a tree's node is, worked out from its counts: entropy in bits and the Gini index, term by term, and what each one counts.

name: entropy-down-a-tree
description: A tree grown by information gain on the 49 cells of 10,000 training digits, all ten classes, to depth 14: 2,033 nodes, 1,017 leaves. The training digits' entropy falls from 3.320 bits at the root to 0.020 at depth 14, and the gains of each depth's splits, each weighted by its node's share, add up to the 3.300 bits removed. Read as a model, a leaf's shares are its predicted probabilities: in nats, the entropy left is exactly the training loss of those shares, at every depth. On 10,000 held-out digits the unsmoothed shares give 1,616 digits probability zero at depth 14, an infinite loss (a held-out 4 lands in a leaf of 439 training 6s), so leaves are smoothed with one imaginary digit of each kind. Then held-out loss falls from 2.302 nats, about ln 10, to 0.691 at depth 10 (82% right) and rises again to 0.712 at depth 14 while training entropy keeps falling; accuracy barely moves after depth 10 (83% at 14). A tree grown by Gini does about as well (best 0.723 nats).
title: Entropy down a tree
summary: A tree grown by information gain spends the root's 3.32 bits question by question; read as a probability model, what is left is its loss in nats.

name: weight-entropy
description: A 784-64-32-10 classifier with 52,650 free parameters, trained for five epochs of Adam from three seeds (10–16% of test digits right before, 96.5–97.0% after). Counted in bins of 0.01, the entropy of all its parameters rises from 4.57 to 5.23 bits each. They spread out 1.50 times, which alone adds 0.59 of the 0.66 bits; rescaled to one spread the two piles differ by 0.07 bits, so as a pile the trained numbers look as random as before. The structure is in where they sit. First-layer weights of neighbouring pixels go from correlation 0.00 to 0.50 and from 0.003 to 0.19 bits of mutual information. The first layer's spectral entropy falls from 5.94 to 5.48 bits (61 to 45 effective directions of 64), the second's from 4.63 to 4.50, while the last layer's stays about the same (3.09 to 3.13). The 67 pixels never lit in training keep their random weights exactly.
title: The entropy of a network's weights
summary: Every free parameter of an MNIST classifier, before and after training: as a pile of numbers its entropy goes up; the structure is in how the numbers are arranged.

name: logits-loss-and-nats
description: The same trained classifier on the 10,000 test digits. Test digit 0, a 7: its logits, 9.51 for 7 and 5.85 for 3, differ by 3.66, the log of the ratio of their probabilities, 0.9745 and 0.0251. Adding a constant to all ten changes nothing. Its loss is −ln 0.9745 = 0.026 nats (0.037 bits). Over all 10,000 the mean loss is 0.113 ± 0.006 nats (0.163 bits), while the median digit's is 0.002. The worst 100 digits carry 42% of the total and the 345 misnamed ones 74%; the worst is a 1 called a 2 with probability 0.00005, 9.86 nats. A uniform guess scores ln 10 = 2.303 nats and the class shares 2.301; the model's perplexity is 1.12. The mean loss is minus the log-likelihood of all 10,000 labels over 10,000: they cost 1,627 bits to send with the model against 33,219 without. Temperature chosen on half the digits is best at 1: it moves the loss and never the accuracy.
title: Logits, loss and nats
summary: A classifier's loss in statistical terms: logits as log-odds, the loss of one digit in nats and bits, the mean as an estimate with an error, and the likelihood it is the negative log of.

name: kl-divergence
description: The classifier of "Logits, loss and nats" (784-64-32-10, seed 0, 96.5% right) as the model q. Its loss on test digit 0, −ln 0.9745 = 0.026 nats, is a cross-entropy CE(p, q) = H(p) + KL(p‖q). For a one-hot label H = 0 and the loss is all KL. For a label-smoothed target (ε = 0.1: 0.91 on the 7, 0.01 on each other digit) the split is 0.500 + 0.623 = 1.123 nats, worked out class by class. 98% of it is the 1% on wrong digits that the model all but ruled out (q(6) = 1.0×10⁻¹⁰ alone costs 0.230), and the KL terms of the 7 and the 3 are negative where q > p. Over the 10,000 test digits the parts add up exactly for three targets: one-hot labels 0 + 0.113 = 0.113, smoothed targets 0.500 + 0.721 = 1.222, and a teacher's soft targets (the same network from seed 1, logits ÷ 2) 0.484 + 0.338 = 0.822. The untrained network has the same H with KL 2.28, 1.78 and 1.79, so training changed only the KL part. KL is not symmetric: KL(q‖p) is 0.222 for smoothed targets and 0.115 for the teacher, and infinite for one-hot labels. One Gaussian fitted to 12,665 training 1s and 0s, placed along the difference of their average pictures (two humps), by forward KL takes p's mean and spread, 2.37 and 3.98, centred where p is 2% of its peak. By reverse KL it sits on the 1s alone (centre −1.22, width 0.46, none of its mass on the 0s). Each fit loses badly on the other measure: 12.5 against 0.70, and 65.5 against 0.78 nats.
title: Cross-entropy is entropy plus KL
summary: A classifier's loss is a cross-entropy: the target's own entropy, which no model can beat, plus the KL divergence, the only part training moves; KL measured on three targets, both ways round, and as a fit to two humps of digits.

name: every-loss-is-a-likelihood
description: A measurement with errors from 500 seeded MNIST training digits: the ink of a digit's right half against its left half's, binned into 9 bins of the left half's ink (495 digits), each bin's mean with its standard error. A straight line fitted by the lowest chi-square has slope 0.832 ± 0.026 (chi-square 14.9 for 7 degrees of freedom). For Gaussian errors −2 ln L is exactly chi-square plus Σ ln 2πσᵢ², here −83.11 at every slope, so the lowest chi-square and the highest likelihood fall at the same slope. The curvature of −ln L, 1,524, gives the slope's error, ±0.026; the slopes of 120 disjoint samples of 500 digits scatter by 0.028 ± 0.002, and their curvature errors average 0.027. With one σ for every digit, chi-square is N/σ² times the mean squared error: least squares on the 500 digits gives a slope of 0.844 and an MSE of 0.000608 (0.000680 on 10,000 held-out digits), and with σ = √MSE chi-square is 500. A softmax regression (784→10, five epochs of plain gradient descent) has a held-out cross-entropy of 0.275 nats (92.3% right): minus the log of the product of the probabilities it gave the 10,000 right digits, about 10⁻¹¹⁹³, over 10,000. A logistic regression of 4 against 9 has a binary cross-entropy of 0.107 nats on 1,991 held-out digits (96.1% right), minus the log of a Bernoulli likelihood; the ten-class model read on its 4 and 9 logits alone gives 0.112. Each loss is the negative log-likelihood of the distribution it assumes.
title: Every loss is a likelihood
summary: Chi-square, squared error and cross-entropy are each minus the log of a likelihood: a line fitted to measured MNIST ink, a softmax regression of ten digits and a logistic regression of two, measured on held-out digits.

name: from-a-cut-to-a-tree
description: MNIST 4s stand for signal and 9s for background, with the two measured features of "Choosing a split"; 8,000 training events, and every efficiency measured on 5,782 held-out ones. Cut on one feature, the ink's vertical spread, s/√(s+b) of the training events is best at 4.90 pixels (3,537 4s and 707 9s kept, 54.3); a tree's root, scoring the same thresholds by Gini gain, picks 4.88, so close that on held-out events they keep 87% and 86% of 4s and 18.0% and 16.1% of 9s. With the 4s made rare, 50 for every 1,000 9s, both move to 4.64. That cut is a tree of depth one; asking again in each half, with either feature, splits the plane into 4, 8, then 32 boxes. Where the cut keeps 86% of held-out 4s it keeps 16.1% of 9s; the depth-5 tree keeps 6.9%, and the likelihood ratio estimated from two 10 × 10 histograms of the training events, the Neyman–Pearson best test, keeps 6.4%. The area under the held-out ROC curve rises from 0.850 for the stump to 0.958 at depth 5, against 0.962 for the ratio, then falls to 0.857 when the tree is grown to the end at depth 27, while on its training events it reaches 1.000.
title: From a cut to a tree
summary: An analysis cut is a tree of depth one; asking again in each half gives a tree whose boxes approach the likelihood ratio, until it grows deep enough to fit noise.

name: dense-layer-learns-local
description: The first layer of the 784-64-32-10 MNIST classifier of "The entropy of a network's weights", read as 64 pictures of 28 × 28 weights. Before training, two weights of a unit are uncorrelated at every distance (0.000 to 0.006). After five epochs they agree with their neighbours: 0.48 one pixel apart along a row or column, 0.32 at two and 0.19 at three, half the one-pixel value by 2.6 pixels, and only 0.01 to 0.03 from 6 pixels on. Each unit still pays for every pixel: 784 × 64 = 50,176 weights. A 3 × 3 convolution with as many maps keeps only the nine near pixels and shares one filter at every position: 9 × 64 = 576 weights, 87 times fewer, for 676 times the outputs (43,264). A dense layer giving that many outputs would need 33,918,976 weights, and a local layer that does not share would need 389,376. Trained on the same 60,000 digits with the same budget (2,340 updates of 128, Adam), a small CNN with 3 × 3 filters (5,258 parameters) and the dense classifier (52,650) name 98.2% and 96.5% of held-out digits. Moved by 1, 2, 3 and 4 pixels, the dense classifier falls to 93%, 73%, 45% and 24%, and the CNN to 97%, 91%, 75% and 51%. A shifted digit's first-layer maps are its maps shifted, exactly; the pooling and dense head that follow are not, so both models still lose digits that move.
title: A dense layer learns to be local
summary: Training gives a dense layer's near pixels similar weights; a 3×3 convolution keeps only those near weights and shares them, using 576 weights instead of 50,176, and loses fewer held-out digits when they move.

name: markov-chain-to-rnn
description: Tables counted from the 892,324-character Tiny Shakespeare training split, orders 0 to 8 with add-α smoothing chosen on validation, scored on 111,474 held-out characters. On the text they were counted from they only improve, from 4.77 bits per character to 1.47. Held out they are best at order 4, 2.85 bits, then get worse, to 4.81 at order 8, where 56% of held-out contexts were never counted (8% at order 4). A GRU with 128 hidden units and 82,881 parameters, trained here in numpy by truncated backpropagation through time (1,200 updates of 64 streams × 64 characters, 5.5 passes, one seed), falls from 6.03 bits untrained to 2.68 held out. It scores 2.22 on training text, a gap of 0.46 against the table's 1.01. The order-4 table stores 125,229 counts of 65⁵ = 1,160,290,625 possible. Where a held-out position's order-4 context was never counted, the table gives every character 1/65 (6.02 bits) and the GRU scores 4.34; where it was counted 1–9 times, 3.35 against 2.87; where it was counted 10 times or more, the two are about even (2.46 against 2.52, and 2.47 against 2.45). As perplexity, 2^bits: 65 for a uniform guess, 28.4 for single characters, 7.2 for the best table and 6.4 for the GRU.
title: From a Markov chain to an RNN
summary: A table of counted contexts must have seen the exact context, so on held-out text it gets worse past a few characters; a small recurrent network carries a state and shares its parameters across contexts, and beats the best table.

name: labels-against-rewards
description: A 784-64-10 classifier trained on MNIST two ways from the same start and on the same batches of 64 for 10,000 Adam updates, three seeds: cross-entropy on the label (gradient on the logits p − onehot(y)), and REINFORCE as a one-step bandit, where a digit drawn from the softmax earns 1 if it is right and 0 if not and the label is never shown (gradient (r − b)(p − onehot(a)), baseline a moving average of past rewards). For one real training digit, a 6 with p(6) = 0.54, the reward's gradient averaged over the draw is exactly 0.536 times the label's (the mean of 10,000 draws is within 0.002): a right guess gives the label's gradient times (1 − b), and a wrong one only pushes that guess down. Over a whole batch the two gradients have a cosine of only 0.28–0.35. A label can carry log₂ 10 = 3.32 bits; the right/wrong reward's entropy peaks at 0.92–1.00 bits and falls to 0.26–0.29 once 95% of guesses are right, so a run's rewards carry 0.25–0.28M bits against its labels' 2.12M. On the 10,000 held-out digits the reward needs 3.5–9.5 times the updates to reach 90% (600–1,900 against 160–200) and ends at 95.0–95.5% against 97.4–97.6%. In one seed of three the rewarded network stopped naming four digits, the 4s from update 100 to 1,700: a digit never guessed is never rewarded.
title: Labels against rewards
summary: The same classifier trained from labels and from a right-or-wrong reward: the same direction on average, at most a bit per digit, and several times the updates.

name: bits-in-a-weight
description: The 784-64-32-10 classifier of "The entropy of a network's weights" (seed 0, 96.55% of test digits right) has its 52,544 weights rounded to each number format, and each is measured three ways: the bits it stores, the entropy of the values the weights take there (what an ideal code would need), and held-out accuracy on the 10,000 test digits. Counted in bins of 0.01 the weights had 5.23 bits each; float32 stores 32, and 52,522 of the 52,544 values differ, so a count can show at most log₂ 52,544 = 15.68 bits. FP16 carries 13.29 of its 16 bits (13,417 values), BF16 10.54 (2,703 values) and FP8 6.28 of 8 (108 values), and all three keep the accuracy (96.55%, 96.55%, 96.49%). In plain FP4, whose smallest nonzero value is 0.5, the 98.1% of weights within 0.25 of zero round to 0: five values, 0.16 bits, and 17.0% right. With one power-of-two scale per 32 weights (8 bits a block, 0.25 bits a weight), FP4 leaves 8.3% at zero, carries 3.86 of its 4 bits and gets 96.2% right. On symmetric integer grids accuracy holds down to 5 bits, 3.61 bits carried (96.6%); at 4 bits (2.54 carried) it is 94.0%, at 3 bits 89.0% and at 2 bits 19.3%.
title: How many bits a weight carries
summary: A trained weight stored in 32 bits carries far fewer: rounded to each number format, the entropy of its values against the accuracy kept, and why plain 4-bit needs a shared scale.

name: counting-weights-dnn-and-cnn
description: The two networks met earlier on the page, counted one layer at a time. A weight is one number the model learns, joining one input to one output, and each output also learns one bias: nn.Linear(1, 1) learns 1 × 1 + 1 = 2 numbers and nn.Linear(3, 2) learns 3 × 2 + 2 = 8. The MLP of "An MLP, step by step" (784-64-32-10) learns 784 × 64 + 64 = 50,240 in its first layer, 64 × 32 + 32 = 2,080 in its second and 32 × 10 + 10 = 330 in its last. Flatten and ReLU learn nothing, so its total is 52,650 (52,544 weights and 106 biases), 95% of them in the first layer. The CNN of "A CNN training step" starts with nn.Conv2d(1, 4, kernel_size=3): four 3 × 3 filters on a grey picture with one channel, 4 × 1 × 3 × 3 + 4 = 40 numbers. Run over a picture of 28 × 28 or 84 × 84, the filters use the same 40 numbers. ReLU, the 2 × 2 max-pool and Flatten learn nothing. Its dense layer reads 4 maps of 13 × 13 = 676 numbers and learns 676 × 10 + 10 = 6,770 of them, 99.4% of the CNN's 6,810, 7.7 times fewer than the MLP. Every count is checked against the size of the models' own parameter arrays, which is what sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()) adds up.
title: Counting the weights: a DNN and a CNN
summary: How many numbers a dense network and a convolutional network learn, counted layer by layer beside the PyTorch line that makes each layer: 52,650 for the MNIST MLP and 6,810 for the small CNN, nearly all of them in one dense layer.

name: counting-weights-transformer
description: How many numbers a transformer learns, counted one part at a time with one rule: each output has one weight per input, plus one bias. Attention first, in the small vision transformer of "A self-attention training step": its query, key, value and output matrices are four blocks of 24 × 24 = 576 weights with no biases, 2,304 in all. Its 3 heads cut each block into pieces of 24 × 8 and add nothing: every number of heads that divides 24 gives 2,304. The rest of that model, part by part: patches to tokens 49 × 24 + 24 = 1,200, a class token of 24, positions 17 × 24 = 408, the MLP 24 × 32 + 32 = 800 and the output layer 32 × 10 + 10 = 330, for 5,066, exactly what its own arrays hold. One block of GPT-2 small, the same way: two LayerNorms of 768 + 768 = 1,536, Q, K and V in one layer of 768 × 2,304 + 2,304 = 1,771,776, the attention output 768 × 768 + 768 = 590,592, and an MLP of 768 × 3,072 + 3,072 = 2,362,368 out and 3,072 × 768 + 768 = 2,360,064 back: 7,087,872. Twelve blocks make 85,054,464. With the token table (50,257 × 768 = 38,597,376), the positions (1,024 × 768 = 786,432) and a final norm (1,536), GPT-2 small learns 124,439,808 numbers, exactly the learned tensors of its released weights. Its output layer reuses the token table, so it adds none. The MLPs hold 46% and the token table 31%. In each block attention holds a third and the MLP two thirds. Each part is shown with the line of PyTorch that makes it, and the count ends with sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()).
title: Counting the weights: a transformer
summary: One rule, one part at a time, counts every weight of a transformer: 2,304 in the small ViT's attention, whatever the number of heads, 5,066 in the whole ViT, 7,087,872 in a GPT-2 block and 124,439,808 in GPT-2 small, whose output layer reuses the token table.

name: blocks-a-tensor
description: One digit as the computer holds it. x, y = train_set[0] gives the first training digit of MNIST, after ToTensor and Normalize((0.1307,), (0.3081,)), and its label, y = 5. It is drawn as a blue card of 28 × 28 tiles, deeper blue for a bigger number. A 3 × 3 patch of the stroke is read out number by number: 1.99, 2.80, 0.47, 0.02, 2.64, 2.44, −0.42, 0.61, 2.63. The paper reads −0.42 (0 − 0.1307, divided by 0.3081) and the darkest ink 2.82. print(x.shape, y) prints torch.Size([1, 28, 28]) 5: 1 channel, 28 rows and 28 columns, so 1 × 28 × 28 = 784 numbers. A tensor is a block of numbers with a shape. The code on screen is examples/mnist_blocks.py, and the numbers are the data as that program loads it.
title: A tensor is a block of numbers
summary: One digit is a tensor: 784 numbers in a block of shape [1, 28, 28], from −0.42 on the paper to 2.82 in the darkest ink.

name: blocks-a-batch
description: DataLoader(train_set, batch_size=64, shuffle=True) gives the model 64 digits at a time. The first batch's 64 digit cards slide one behind the other into one block, then their 64 labels fill a row: 0, 8, 6, 7, 4, 3, 9, 1, 1, 1 and so on. x, y = next(iter(loader)) and print(x.shape, y.shape) give torch.Size([64, 1, 28, 28]) and torch.Size([64]): 64 × 784 = 50,176 numbers in one block. The shuffle mixes the digits: this batch holds every digit, from 9 ones and 9 threes down to 3 sixes and 3 eights.
title: A batch: many digits in one block
summary: 64 digits slide into one block of shape [64, 1, 28, 28] and their labels into a row of 64: 50,176 numbers handed to the model at once.

name: blocks-flatten
description: nn.Flatten(), the first block of the course's model, unrolls each 28 × 28 digit row by row into one strip of 784 numbers: row 0, then row 1, and so on, the count rising 28, 56, … 784. The tile in row 14, column 15 goes to place 14 × 28 + 15 = 407, and its number, 2.80, stays the same. Over the whole first batch, [64, 1, 28, 28] becomes [64, 784]: 64 strips, one per digit, one under the other. Flatten learns 0 numbers; it only changes the shape.
title: Flatten: a square becomes a strip
summary: nn.Flatten unrolls each 28 × 28 digit row by row into a strip of 784, so [64, 1, 28, 28] becomes [64, 784], and it learns nothing.

name: blocks-a-linear-layer
description: One output of nn.Linear(784, 64), worked out with the course model's own numbers after one epoch of SGD. The first digit of the first batch, a 0, arrives from Flatten as a strip of 784 numbers. The layer is a grid of 64 rows of 784 orange weight tiles (784 × 64 = 50,176 weights) and a thin strip of 64 biases. Row 8 lights up and is copied under the strip so that matching numbers line up. The three biggest products are read out: 2.82 × 0.101 = 0.28, 2.80 × 0.078 = 0.22 and 2.76 × 0.072 = 0.20. A marker runs along all 784 products, adding them up to 8.09, and adding the bias, −0.02, gives 8.07, the biggest of the 64 outputs. Every row does the same, so the digit's 64 outputs fill a row and the batch's [64, 784] comes out as [64, 64].
title: nn.Linear: a grid of weights
summary: One output of nn.Linear(784, 64) is the digit's 784 numbers times one row of weights, added up, plus a bias: 8.09 − 0.02 = 8.07.

name: blocks-relu
description: nn.ReLU() on the 64 numbers nn.Linear(784, 64) gave the first digit of the first batch, in the course model after one epoch: 33 of them are below 0. Eight are read out: 8.07, −0.15, 1.53, 0.71, 2.51, 2.36, −2.98 and −1.00. One at a time, each negative one turns into a grey 0 while the positive ones pass unchanged, and then the rest of the row follows: 33 of 64 become 0. The shape stays [64, 64], and ReLU learns no numbers: it is a rule, not a grid of weights. Over the whole first batch, 1,954 of 4,096 numbers become 0 (48%), and over all 60,000 training digits, 49%.
title: nn.ReLU: negatives become 0
summary: nn.ReLU turns every negative number into 0 and learns nothing: 48% of the first batch's hidden numbers and 49% over all 60,000 digits.

name: blocks-a-model-is-a-stack
description: nn.Sequential stacks six blocks into the course's 784-64-32-10 digit classifier. They are built one by one as the lines of examples/mnist_blocks.py run: Flatten (a blue card with no weights), Linear(784, 64) (its trained weights as orange tiles), ReLU (grey), Linear(64, 32), ReLU and Linear(32, 10). On the first batch, each block hands the next a new shape: [64, 1, 28, 28] in, then [64, 784], [64, 64], [64, 64], [64, 32], [64, 32] and [64, 10]. That is 784 → 64 → 32 → 10 numbers per digit. print(model) writes the same six blocks, numbered 0 to 5, shown in full beside the stack. Only the three Linear blocks learn numbers: 50,240 + 2,080 + 330 = 52,650, which print(sum(p.numel() for p in params)) prints, as counted in "Counting the weights: a DNN and a CNN".
title: A model is a stack of blocks
summary: nn.Sequential stacks Flatten, Linear and ReLU into the 784-64-32-10 digit classifier, whose three Linear blocks learn all 52,650 numbers.

name: blocks-conv2d
description: nn.Conv2d(1, 4, 3) makes 4 stamps of 3 × 3 weights, shown here as a fresh layer starts them: random numbers between −1/3 and 1/3, not trained. On the first digit of the first batch (a 0), one stamp covers the 3 × 3 pixels at row 20, column 15. Each pixel is multiplied by its weight and the 9 products add up to −0.38; the bias, −0.04, brings it to −0.42, one number of a new sheet. The same stamp then slides over all 26 × 26 = 676 places, using the same 9 numbers every time, and fills the sheet. Four stamps make four sheets, so maps = conv(x) turns [64, 1, 28, 28] into [64, 4, 26, 26]. The layer learns 4 × 3 × 3 + 4 = 40 numbers, the same 40 for a picture of any size. Every number is exact arithmetic on the real digit, checked against direct loops and against PyTorch's own nn.Conv2d.
title: nn.Conv2d: one small stamp, used everywhere
summary: One 3 × 3 stamp of 9 weights slides over all 676 places of a digit; 4 stamps make 4 sheets, [64, 4, 26, 26], from just 40 learned numbers.

name: blocks-pooling
description: nn.MaxPool2d(2) on the first sheet that nn.Conv2d made from a real digit (the untrained stamps of the animation before). The sheet is cut into 2 × 2 squares, and each square becomes one number, its biggest. In the square at row 18, column 18 the four numbers are −1.00, 0.37, 0.47 and 1.34, so 1.34 is kept. Square after square, all 13 × 13 = 169 squares make a sheet of 13 × 13. Over the 4 sheets of every digit, small = pool(maps) turns [64, 4, 26, 26] into [64, 4, 13, 13]: 2,704 numbers per digit become 676, a quarter. The block learns 0 numbers; it only picks. The arithmetic is exact, checked against a direct loop and against PyTorch's nn.MaxPool2d.
title: nn.MaxPool2d: keep the biggest
summary: nn.MaxPool2d(2) keeps the biggest of each 2 × 2 square (1.34 of −1.00, 0.37, 0.47 and 1.34), so 26 × 26 sheets become 13 × 13, a quarter of the numbers, and it learns nothing.

name: blocks-dropout
description: nn.Dropout(0.2) in the course's dropout run: the digit classifier with nn.Dropout(0.2) after each ReLU, trained one epoch with SGD. The 64 numbers h of the first digit after the first ReLU (30 of them already 0) meet the switches that run really drew. In training, drop(h) switches 15 of the 64 off at random and makes the others 1 / (1 − 0.2) = 1.25 times bigger (0.93 becomes 1.16). Every step picks a new set, 12 then 15 off, and over the epoch 768,326 of 3,840,000 switches were off, 20.0%. In eval() nothing is switched off and drop(h) gives back h. On the 10,000 held-out digits, the model left in training mode gets 91.90% right (9,190); after model.eval() it gets 94.35% (9,435), 245 more. The switches are checked to reproduce the run's first loss exactly. The accuracies are measured.
title: nn.Dropout: switched off at random
summary: nn.Dropout(0.2) switches 1 in 5 numbers off at random while training (15 of 64 at the first step) and none after model.eval(), which, measured, gets 94.35% of held-out digits right against 91.90% when it is forgotten.

name: blocks-normalisation
description: The same block of numbers normalised two ways. h is the course model's real hidden layer for the first batch: 64 digits (rows) by 64 features (columns), after one epoch of training, 48% of them 0 after ReLU.
